description: Shared vocabulary. Every question (skill, core, or applied) lives in questions/<id>.json and every word problem in word-problems/<id>.json. Both are written in one step language: a step is something a student does, steps run in sequence, `all` marks steps that can be done in any order, `choose` marks a decision with alternatives, and `use` calls another question. build.py turns this into first-step trees for a classifier and into diagrams that follow one graph grammar.

kinds.skill: A small building block that other questions call; also practiceable on its own.
kinds.core: A question type with its own methods; may also be called as a skill (missing-value rewrites a fraction over a new denominator).
kinds.applied: A core question in context, declared with `reduces_to`: which core question, how the variables map, how answers translate, and what the core methods are called here. May add methods of its own.

question_fields.title: short name
question_fields.prompt: student-facing template; {name} is replaced by the value
question_fields.quantities: groups of inputs that form one quantity (one fraction, one offer); a step that uses one group is 'within', more than one is 'across'
question_fields.outputs: names a method must produce; most questions produce `answer`
question_fields.default_method: used when a value is needed and the method doesn't matter (e.g. a question that calls itself)
question_fields.examples: [{id, values, answer}]; `answer` is an object when there are several outputs
question_fields.methods: the top-level choice: method id → {name, idea, best_when?, watch_out?, answer_relation?, decides?, steps}
question_fields.reduces_to: applied only: {question, with, say, answer_map?, note?, methods: 'all' | {core_id: {id?, name?, idea?}}}
question_fields.mental_first_steps: first steps students often do in their head; the step after one of them is also accepted as a first step

every_step.say: the sentence for the step, e.g. 'Multiply across the diagonal'; may use {name} for values. The worked expression (4 × 18 = 72) is generated, not written.

primitive.op: add | subtract | multiply | divide | gcf | lcm | plot | compare | floor_div | mod | map
primitive.args: names, numeric literals, or [x, y] pairs
primitive.hidden: bookkeeping a student wouldn't write (no `say` needed)
primitive.requires_integer / requires_nonnegative: the method doesn't apply when the result isn't whole / is negative

use.question: id of the question to call
use.method: optional: force one of its methods
use.with: callee input → caller name or literal

all.branches: [[steps], [steps], …]: every branch is done, in any order; a student may start with any of them

choose.options: [{say, correct: true | trap: 'the mistake', …effects}]; exactly one option is correct, the rest are traps. Used for extraction decisions.

steps.search: on a multiply step: {var, until: [out, target]} | {var, until_power_of_ten: out} | {var, until_divisible_by: [out, divisor]}; var tries 1, 2, 3, … (a ratio table, listing multiples)

repeat.choose: {var, any: 'common_factor', of: [x, y]} picked fresh each round
repeat.steps: sub-steps run each round; stops when no common factor is left

steps.compare: args are two values (or two [x, y] pairs); `meaning` maps '=', '<', '>' (or '≠' as fallback) to the answer
steps.map: {op: 'map', args: [name], table: {from: to}, hidden: true}; translates an answer

answer_relation.multiple: the method may return a multiple of the expected answer (the product of two numbers is a common multiple, not always the least)

decides.equality_only: the method can show two things are equal or not, but not which is bigger; its answer is 'not equal' when they differ

levels.note: Dividing by a common factor counts as 'factor'.
the exact expression, e.g. divide(a, b)

classification.tie_break: When methods share a first step, the tree branches on the second step. If the first two steps are the same, the entry keeps several methods.

graph_grammar.description: Every diagram is drawn from the step language with the same node and edge types, and carries a legend at the bottom.

nodes.start: rounded: the question with its numbers, or the story
nodes.step: rectangle: one thing the student does; line 1 is the sentence (`say`), line 2 the worked expression, line 3 tags in brackets: [operation · scope] for a first step, [in: <question>] for a step inside a call
nodes.call: box with side bars: another question used as one step, with what goes in and what comes out; it has its own page
nodes.choice: hexagon marked ×: the student picks one way forward; this is where the classifier works
nodes.all: diamond marked 'all': split into branches that are all done in any order; a second diamond joins them
nodes.wrong_end: rounded, red: where a trap leads, with the first steps that give it away
nodes.frame: a labeled box around an expanded call (the extraction, or the question inside a word problem)

edges.option: arrow leaving a choice, always labeled with the option: the method it leads to, or the extraction answer (✓ correct)
edges.trap: red dashed arrow leaving a choice, labeled ✗ with the concept and the wrong answer chosen
edges.data: thick arrow into a call or frame, labeled with the values passed in (a: 4 spoons of sugar)

graph_grammar.methods: A method is a named route, not a node. Steps that methods share are drawn once; a choice node sits where the routes split, and the method's name is on the option edge where the route becomes unique.

tree_files.match.args: expression strings over the question's inputs: a name ('a'), a number ('100'), an operation ('divide(a, b)'), or a wildcard: 'int' (any whole number the student chose) or 'common_factor(x, y)' (any number > 1 dividing both). Second-step args can refer to first-step results, e.g. 'multiply(divide(a, b), d)'. Evaluate them with the problem's values and compare to the student's numbers.
matching_rules: Parse the student's step into (op, numbers).
Try entries with no wildcards first.
Ignore argument order for add, multiply, gcf, lcm.
Steps inside `all` blocks appear in every order, so a student may start with either fraction.
If the entry lists several methods, match the student's next step against `next`.
